correctness.rationale: All four caps cover exactly when their convex hull contains the origin-centred ball of radius \(\cos w\). Euler’s tetrahedral inequality fixes the unique two labelled rotation orbits at \(w_0=rccos(1/3)\). A regular-tetrahedron local chart has five symmetric trace-free deformations and three rotations, with verified nonsingular Gram determinant \(J=2048/243\). Facet offsets have derivative \(8L_i/27\) and common diagonal quadratic loss \(2Q/9\); the small event forces off-diagonal modes \(O(\delta)\) and diagonal modes \(O(\sqrt\delta)\). Integrating the exact limiting tetrahedral region yields \(19683\sqrt3\pi\delta^4/512\) and normalized probability coefficient \(81\sqrt3/(4\pi)\). The exact conversion from \(\delta\) to angular excess yields \(16\sqrt3/\pi\). A separately implemented geometric-face checker reproduces the tangent Jacobian, Taylor coefficients and convergence of rescaled event volumes. The argument explicitly separates finite numerics from the analytic limit.

originality.rationale: The closest full primary source, Finch (arXiv:1502.06931, 2015), explicitly treats this same four-random-cap coverage probability below a hemisphere but gives no lower-endpoint asymptotic and states the global exact expression remains unknown; its available lower bounds start near 84 degrees. Bürgisser–Cucker–Lotz (arXiv:0712.2816, 2007) give exact expressions for caps at least hemispherical and upper bounds for smaller caps, not a sharp tetrahedral onset. The independent five-parameter localization and coefficient \(16\sqrt3/\pi\) are not implied by those stated results. The general deterministic tetrahedral inequality is prior mathematics used as input. Overlap with available records was checked at the statement/implication level. An older formula or unindexed calculation could still yield the claim, so historical priority is provisional.

value.rationale: Four caps is the minimum number capable of covering \(S^2\), and the tetrahedral covering radius is the natural sharp geometric threshold. The result resolves the previously zero-known lower-endpoint probability to leading order, with an exact nontrivial coefficient and exponent. The quartic exponent reflects a geometrically meaningful rank split (three first-order and two second-order shape modes) rather than a routine substitution, arbitrary truncation or numerical approximation.
